description: Lightning is not magic: it is a huge electrical discharge in a storm cloud. Here's how she prepares, then how she hits.

hero.hook: In a fraction of a second, the air rises to 30,000°C. Five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.

blocks.text: A lightning bolt releases colossal energy in the blink of an eye. The air in the lightning channel rises to approximately **30,000 °C**. Thunder is just the sound of this brutal heat.
To understand lightning, you have to follow three steps: how the cloud gets charged, how the electricity finds a path, and why you hear thunder afterwards.
Lightning occurs mainly in : very large storm clouds, which can rise to around **15 km**. Inside, the air rises and falls very strongly. [[cumulonimbus]]

In this chaos, small **ice crystals** rise, and heavier ice grains () descend. When they collide, electrical charges are exchanged. Little by little, the top of the cloud becomes rather positive, the base rather negative. [[sleet]]
Lake Maracaibo, in Venezuela, is one of the most lightning-hit places on the planet: almost daily storms are observed there for a large part of the year.

Air is a bad conductor. But if the difference in charge becomes too great (often **hundreds of millions of volts**), the air ends up giving way. Molecules lose electrons: they become conductive. It's the . [[Air ionization]]
An invisible channel leaves the cloud in small leaps. From the ground, electric nets rise especially from points (trees, lightning rods, buildings). When the two come together, the circuit closes.

The great light that we see, the **arc back**, rises mainly from the ground towards the cloud. The current can reach tens of thousands of amps. Several discharges can follow one another in the same channel: hence the flickering effect.

sections.title: When the air lets go: the discharge

blocks.text: The lightning heats the air so quickly that it suddenly expands. This shock wave becomes **thunder**. The light comes almost immediately; the sound advances at approximately **340 m/s**.
Simple tip: count the seconds between lightning and thunder, then divide by **3**. You get an estimate of the distance in kilometers.
The Earth is struck by approximately **100 lightning bolts per second** on average. In France, there are around **one million** impacts on the ground per year.

Lightning remains dangerous, especially outdoors, near isolated trees or water. It also starts fires. But it has a lesser known effect: it helps produce nitrogen compounds that fertilize the soil with rain.
Above the storms, cameras also captured bizarre phenomena, such as : brief glows in the upper atmosphere, invisible to the naked eye from the ground. [[Leprechauns]]
In a cumulonimbus, ice/sleet collisions separate the charges. When the voltage becomes too high, the air is ionized: the lightning heats up to ~30,000°C, and this sudden expansion produces thunder.
